title: A Place at the Table
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 22 of 40
content:
The chair had been empty all week.

I didn't notice that until Mina tried to move it.

The Jasmine Dragon was between its lunch rush and the afternoon regulars, that strange hour when the shop looked empty but every cup still needed washing. Mina had a mop in one hand and a stack of accounts in the other. The chair occupied the only clear stretch between the long table and the counter.

"Can this go upstairs?" she asked.

Iroh, elbow-deep in the tea tins, looked up so quickly I thought he'd heard an alarm.

"That chair stays."

Mina lowered the mop. "It can't stay there and let me reach the storeroom."

"It was always there."

"So was the cracked floor tile. I fixed that."

I hid a smile in my cup. The chair was ordinary, with a rubbed patch on one arm and a cushion that had been mended twice. Somebody had written an old number underneath it. I had assumed it belonged to the shop, like the kettles and the stubborn front latch.

When Mina returned to the counter, I asked Iroh who used to sit there.

"Many people."

"Do they still?"

"Sometimes."

He answered in the soft, complete voice he used when he didn't want to answer at all. I could have let it go. I could also see Mina shifting the mop around the obstruction again.

"If you're keeping it for someone," I said, "that's okay. But does it have to block everybody else?"

Iroh folded a cloth over the counter. "It belonged to an old customer who came here when the city was less kind."

"Did they ask you to save it?"

He studied the worn armrest.

"No."

I didn't press for the name. The story could belong partly to somebody who wasn't here to give permission for it to be told.

Mina came back with a tray of bowls. "The carpenter can fix the loose joint for four copper," she said. "I asked. If it stays downstairs, we need room around it. If it goes upstairs, the stairs are narrow. I'm not carrying it alone."

"Neither should you," I said.

Iroh smiled faintly. "I have been informed that my furniture is demanding a council."

"Your furniture isn't demanding anything," Mina said. "Your employees are."

That landed.

Iroh asked whether we could close the shop for half an hour and rearrange the table together. Mina said no: there was still an advertised tea tasting at three, and closing early would mean losing customers she'd already prepared for. We could move the chairs after the tasting, when she was being paid to work anyway.

I loved that she didn't make his kindness into an excuse to work for free.

The afternoon group arrived early. A little girl with her grandmother sat at the long table, and an old porter occupied the chair beside the window. When he saw the empty seat, he asked whether he could use it.

Iroh opened his mouth.

I watched him decide.

"Please do," he said.

The porter sat. He didn't become a symbol of healing. He complained about the weak tea, bought a second cup and left a respectable tip. When he rose, he thanked Mina instead of Iroh, because she was the one who had served him.

Later we moved the chair closer to the others. The aisle was wide enough for Mina's cart and the tray she carried at closing. The carpenter would repair the joint on market day. Iroh paid the deposit from the shop account and wrote the amount in the ledger so she wouldn't have to chase him for it.

The carpenter arrived with a notebook and a square of dark wood for testing the joint. He asked who had the authority to approve work on the shop furniture.

"I do," Iroh said.

"And the clear aisle?" Mina asked.

The carpenter looked at her. She showed him how she moved the tea cart through the room, including the turn by the kitchen door that had been blocked whenever the chair stood at its old angle.

"Then we need to measure it with the cart," he said.

Iroh stepped back to let them work. He looked almost bereaved by the empty space, though he knew the chair would return after its repair.

"Do you want to tell me whose chair it was?" I asked.

"It belonged to someone who came to the shop when the city was less kind," he said. "He liked sitting where he could see the door. I kept it there after he stopped visiting."

I didn't ask whether the man had died or simply gone elsewhere. Iroh could decide which parts were ready to be shared.

"The people who use the shop now need the aisle," I said.

"I know. Sometimes I confuse preserving a memory with preserving its furniture."

Mina returned with the cart, which passed the new position without touching the table. The carpenter made a mark in his book and said he'd bring the repaired joint after market day. He named a price. Iroh paid the deposit and thanked him for checking the actual path.

When we were alone, Iroh picked up the worn cushion.

"Do you think a person can be loved without a place being held empty forever?"

"Yes," I said. "I hope so. I've been clear that I'm ethically non-monogamous and prefer polyamory. I don't want anyone else's memory removed to make space for me, and I don't want a space reserved as though I have no right to leave."

He folded the cushion into his arms. "That is a great deal of freedom for a chair."

"Your chairs are terribly political."

He laughed. It was a small, relieved laugh, and when he reached for my hand I was glad he had chosen to do it.

I carried the cushions into the back room. He followed with the mended one.

"I liked leaving a place for people to return to," he said.

"You can. But they might want a different seat when they do."

He rubbed a thumb along the seam. "I suppose I kept believing that if nothing changed, I could prove they hadn't been forgotten."

"Did it help?"

"Sometimes."

I set the cushion down. "I don't want to be a person you need to keep a chair empty for."

He looked at me.

"I've told you I prefer polyamory, and that I'm ethically non-monogamous," I said. "That means I may leave for visits and return. It also means I choose where I'm sitting when I get back. You don't have to freeze the shop to make room for me."

"I know your heart is not a reservation," he said.

"Good, because your reservation system is terrible."

He laughed. It started in his chest and worked its way into his face until I was laughing too.

"Then will you accept an invitation to dinner?" he asked.

"With you?"

"I was hoping."

"Ask me after Mina's shift ends. I want to help with the dishes we used, not all the dishes she was hired to wash."

Mina appeared in the doorway. "That may be the most romantic thing anyone has said in this shop."

I blushed so hard I nearly dropped the cushion.

At closing, Iroh cooked a small supper from what he'd actually bought for us. He did not raid the next day's stock to impress me. We sat at the long table, where the repaired chair would go, and he let me serve the first bowl.

"Are you comfortable?" I asked.

"Very."

"Are you about to get up to help a stranger?"

"Only if a stranger falls through the ceiling."

"Reasonable exception."

He reached for my hand across the table. When I moved closer, he asked whether he might kiss me. The kiss was slow and warm and tasted faintly of ginger. We closed the shop together and went upstairs without making the evening into a promise about all the evenings afterward.

The next morning, the chair wasn't empty.

Mina was sitting in it, counting the change from the till. Iroh poured her tea before she asked. Nobody suggested she give up her seat.
